extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, state regulators, utility stakeholders, and legal/policy analysts (notice-and-comment participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed notice-and-comment legal and technical critique of EPA's proposed 111(d) emission guidelines for existing electric generating units (EGUs), focusing on Building Blocks 1 and 2 (heat rate improvement and NGCC redispatch). Identifies required analytic, legal, and factual standards EPA must meet to justify proposed goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat rate improvements must reflect actual unit efficiency changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported heat rate improvements must result from purposeful efforts to improve unit efficiency, not from changes in monitoring/reporting methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cichanowicz review found reported heat rate improvements for many units 'resulted almost exclusively from changes in continuous emission monitoring system (“CEMS”) reporting methodology or stack flow monitor calibration rather than from purposeful efforts to improve unit efficiency.' EPA should therefore validate that reported improvements correspond to real efficiency gains (e.g., verified equipment upgrades), not merely CEMS calibration or reporting changes. Examples: CEMS probe calibration, replacement of stack flow monitors, or changes in CEMS operation produced apparent reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studies used to justify HRI must provide valid documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must present valid, documented studies to rationally justify any proposed heat rate improvement (HRI) goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA argues 'EPA has presented no valid documentation regarding the Sixteen Unit Study on which it can rationally justify any of the proposed options for HRI across the coal-fired EGU fleet.' EPA should not rely on misinterpreted or methodologically flawed studies (e.g., S&L, Sixteen Unit Study) and should address criticisms (UARG, NRECA Nine-Unit Analysis) before adopting HRI mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: CEMS data require careful scrutiny; CEMS changes can bias heat rate estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat rate estimates derived from CEMS can be biased by changes in CEMS operation, calibration, or location and therefore must be interpreted with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comments document numerous examples where gross heat rate reductions were due to CEMS probe calibration, replacement of flow monitors, changes in CEMS location, or apportionment of common-stack CEMS data. EPA should examine whether gross heat rate reductions are artifacts of CEMS measurement changes, compare CEMS-derived heat rates to net heat rate based on coal use (which may differ by 5-10%), and control for CEMS-related measurement variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apportion common-stack CEMS data assuming identical heat rates
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple units share a stack, apportioning CEMS heat input data by load on the assumption of identical heat rates undermines conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's conclusions are 'compromised by using as heat input data ... common stack CEMS and apportioned by load, based on assumed identical hear rate.' Year-to-year differences in unit operating conditions and non-identical heat rates across units must be accounted for; otherwise apportionment creates spurious trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate heat input basis (coal-use based net heat rate vs. CEMS-derived)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should compare CEMS-derived gross heat rate to net heat rate computed from fuel use and account for discrepancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes net heat rate based on coal use exceeded CEMS-derived values by 5-10% in some cases and that CEMS gross heat rate data may be lower than unit design basis. EPA should evaluate both measures and justify which is used for HRI estimation, documenting measurement biases and reconciliations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affected facility for NSPS evaluation comprises the boiler island only
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of NSPS (§60.40Da) and reconstruction/modification analysis, the 'affected facility' for coal-fired EGUs is the steam generating unit (boiler island).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing EPA's Rasnic memo, a steam generating unit includes: (1) fuel combustion system (bunkers, pulverizers, crushers, burners), (2) combustion air system, (3) steam generating system (firebox, boiler tubes), and (4) draft system (excluding the stack). 'The affected facility then starts at the coal bunkers, and ends at the stack breeching.' EPA must adhere to this boundary when evaluating HRI and NSPS applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements outside the boiler island cannot be included in HRI mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Components outside the boiler island (e.g., turbine island, water treatment, main steam piping) are 'outside the fence line' and cannot legally form the basis for EPA's HRI mandates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proposed Rule must distinguish between 'source' components and the affected facility; only boiler island components have historically been part of the affected facility. EPA cannot legally require HRI measures that rely on improvements to excluded components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiable and verifiable HRI expectations for the affected facility
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected HRI associated with the boiler island must be large enough to be quantifiable and verifiable; minimal gains that cannot be quantified should not be used to set standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA S&L study concludes only minimal HRI is associated with boiler island upgrades; if HRI is too small to quantify or verify, it cannot serve as a reliable basis for regulatory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude natural gas simple-cycle (NGSC) HRI due to limited applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: NGSC units should be excluded from HRI obligations where they provide only a marginal share of generation and frequently cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proposed Rule correctly excludes NGSC HRI because NGSC provided ~1% of fossil fuel-fired generation and cycles on and off frequently, making HRI attempts largely impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions about NGCC capacity (70% target) must be evidence-based
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's assumption that existing NGCC units can be operated at a 70% capacity factor fleet-wide must be supported by robust, representative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA based the 70% figure on a small fraction of units achieving that level in limited datasets. The 70% target is arbitrary absent demonstration that the vast majority of NGCC units can reliably and legally operate at that capacity given technical, contractual, and market realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include only EGUs eligible under §111(d)/NSPS in state goal calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: State goals may be established only for existing sources that would be subject to a standard if they were new sources; EPA must limit calculations to those EGUs meeting NSPS eligibility criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSPS for new EGUs applies to turbines with base load rating >73 MW and meeting output/sales thresholds (one-third of potential output and >219,000 MWh three-year average). Including ineligible units in state goal computations inflates expected redispatch and is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not count not-yet-operational NGCC capacity as available for redispatch
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must not treat units that do not currently exist or are not fully developed as available NGCC capacity in state goal calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Deer Creek Station in South Dakota was treated as having an additional 69% available when it was newly operating at ~1% capacity. Such units should be classified appropriately (e.g., 'under construction') or use baseline years reflecting true operational status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use net summer capacity, not nameplate capacity, to estimate available NGCC generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Net summer capacity (actual summer net capacity) better reflects the maximum output available for redispatch than nameplate capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nameplate capacity overstates available generation because it doesn't account for auxiliary loads, station service, and summer derates. The comments provide Florida as an example where using nameplate vs. net summer capacity dramatically alters required capacity factors (70% on nameplate may imply ~86.8% on net summer capacity). EPA must use net summer capacity in state goal computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical capacity factors and plant capability before assuming utilization increases
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must examine historical capacity factor data and whether plants have the demonstrated ability to operate at proposed higher utilization rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperative NGCC plants averaged low capacity factors (e.g., 35% in 2012, 27% in 2013); only a minority operated above 50-60%. Without evidence of technical plant capability, fuel and transport availability, or necessary upgrades, it is irrational to assume units can double historic performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for operating permit limits, fuel usage caps, and design duty constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory permit limits, contractual fuel limits, and units designed for cycling may cap maximum operations below proposed targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some units have mass emission limits or fuel usage caps that effectively prevent operations at 70% capacity. Others were financed and designed for cycling duty; achieving high continuous capacity may require significant retrofits, testing, and investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undermining grid flexibility and reliability by forcing uniform redispatch
rubrics_metrics.description: Redispatch assumptions must respect the differentiated roles of generating resources (flexibility vs. baseload); forcing all NGCC units to base-load can reduce system reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA warns that requiring NGCC plants routinely to operate at high capacity removes regional flexibility (like forcing an investment portfolio into a single asset class), could force cycling of inflexible plants at high cost, and might curtail variable emission-free generation due to lack of firming resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate feasibility by addressing infrastructure constraints (pipelines, storage, costs, timelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must account for the additional gas transportation capacity, pipeline miles, storage capacity, and capital costs required to support increased NGCC generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites INGAA and NERA projections (e.g., tens of thousands of pipeline miles; billions per year in capital expenditures; need for ~1.4 TCF new working gas storage). EPA's 3.5 TCF incremental gas demand estimate should be reconciled with realistic buildout timelines and costs. Pipeline cost and regional variability (e.g., NE vs SW) must be included in feasibility and cost analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on vague 'flexible implementation' to excuse infrastructure lead times
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cannot assume that flexible implementation will allow meaningful delays in infrastructure buildout without affecting interim compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because state interim compliance is based on 2020-2029 averages and EPA assumed Building Blocks implemented by 2020, delaying infrastructure will increase interim emissions and/or force more drastic later reductions. States may thus need infrastructure in place by 2020.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for FERC and other statutory/regulatory constraints on pipeline construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Interstate natural gas pipeline construction requires FERC review and authorizations and numerous federal/state approvals which constrain the ability to rapidly expand capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERC typically requires firm customer commitments before authorizing new capacity; pipelines cannot shift costs to existing customers. Multiple environmental and land-use statutes (CAA, CWA, ESA, CZMA, etc.) and stakeholder opposition can prolong permitting. EPA must factor regulatory timelines and limitations into infrastructure feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider gas-electric interdependencies and fuel delivery reliability (e.g., Polar Vortex impacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interconnection between gas and electric systems (pipeline congestion, priority service for heating) can limit NGCC availability during peak periods and stress reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: during the Polar Vortex, pipelines prioritized heating loads, issuing advisories that constrained power plant fuel deliveries. EPA must consider these operational interdependencies and the potential for fuel shortfalls when evaluating redispatch feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base redispatch potential on units located in different RTOs or with different ownership/customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Redispatch assumptions must respect regional market boundaries and ownership structures; units in different RTOs or serving different customers may not be available to replace in-state coal generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Deer Creek Station and Big Stone are in different RTOs with different owners and customers; re-dispatch between them is not realistically available for a single state's compliance. EPA should account for RTO membership and market constraints in redispatch calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analyses must control for cycling, fuel blending, and year-to-year operational variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed year-to-year heat rate variability can be driven by coal blends, unit cycling (e.g., to follow wind), or annual operating condition changes; analyses must control for these factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antelope Valley Unit 2 experienced large heat rate variation due to following wind energy. EPA's matrix and statistical studies (Sixteen Unit Study, S&L report) failed to adequately control for such operational drivers, leading to misleading HRI estimates.
